newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: Ex-military ruler tops polls in Bolivia.
newsitem.headline: Ex-military ruler tops polls in Bolivia.

text.p: Bolivians vote on Sunday in polls likely to return to office Hugo Banzer, a general who still takes pride in his seven years of iron-fisted military rule during which he crushed leftist guerrillas in the 1970s.
"My conscience is clear," the 71-year-old Banzer said this week. And last week he said, "They were no little angels."

Opinion polls show Banzer, of the right-wing Nationalist Democratic Alliance (ADN), leading the pack with 25-30 percent of the vote, followed by ex-President Jaime Paz Zamora of the Revolutionary Left Movement (MIR) with 15-20 percent.

But no candidate is likely to garner enough ballots to win the Sunday vote in land-locked Bolivia, one of the poorest countries in Latin America, and the next leader will be picked by Congress in early August from between the top two contenders.
Juan Carlos Duran of the ruling centre-right Nationalist Revolutionary Movement (MNR) and Ivo Kuljis of the populist Solidarity Civic Union (UCS) are vying for third place, with Duran slightly ahead.

Ironically, drugs are not a major campaign issue in this Andean nation, which along with Peru and Colombia produces virtually all the world's coca leaf and cocaine, most of which finds its way to the inner-city streets of the United States.

Narcotics come up mostly in relation to Paz Zamora, who has been denied a visa by the White House for his alleged drug- trafficking links. One of outgoing President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada's favourite lines is that if Paz Zamora wins, Bolivia will become an international pariah.
However, no formal charges have been brought against Paz Zamora, who says the scandal was fabricated by his rivals.
In any case, coca is part of everyday life for millions of native Bolivians, who chew its leaves or drink them in tea and who see the cocaine problem as just a "gringo" aberration.

All top candidates have espoused the country's 12-year-old free-market and privatisation drive, which has consistently elicited praise of the international financial community but which appears to be testing the limits of Bolivians' patience.

More than any other contender, Banzer was able to exploit the growing popular discontent with railways, telephones and other services. Rates for these services have shot up since they were privatised, some say beyond the reach of most Bolivians, 70 percent of whom live under the poverty line.

Banzer vows to cut short the seven years of monopoly privatised firms were granted. While the business community dismisses those claims as mere electioneering and say they trust in his free-market slant, analysts say the pledge is music to the ears of Bolivians who demand a change of tack.

"People just want to get rid of Sanchez de Lozada's party," said Humberto Vacaflor, publisher of the Siglo 21 newsletter. Ironically, by leading a successful political obliteration campaign against Paz Zamora, the ruling party left voters with Banzer as the only alternative, he said.

Since he was ousted in 1978 in one of Bolivia's 190 coups, Banzer has run five times for office. Finally winning the popular vote in 1985, he failed to garner a strong-enough majority and was defeated in the second round in Congress.

One candidate who has not embraced the free market is Remedios Loza Alvarado, who campaigns in the typical Colla Indian outfit favoured by many in Bolivia, where more than half the population are pure-blooded Indians who still uphold the customs and speak the language of their ancestors.
"If you give me your vote, I will rule for Bolivians, not for foreigners," she vowed this week. Although polls show her in fifth place nationwide, she could sweep the vote in La Paz.
Besides the president and vice-president, whose term will now be five years instead of four, Bolivians will also choose all 27 senators and 130 deputies.
